candidato.resumo: The New England Journal of Medicine has published a study on the long-term efficacy of AAV8-mediated gene therapy (GNT0003) in patients with Crigler-Najjar syndrome, an extremely rare congenital liver disorder affecting approximately 500 people in Europe. It is caused by a deficiency of UGT1A1, an enzyme required for bilirubin metabolism. The accumulation of this substance can lead to irreversible neurological damage and, in the most severe cases, death.

texto_fonte:
Crigler-Najjar syndrome: Gene therapy maintains its efficacy four years after treatment
The New England Journal of Medicine has published a study on the long-term efficacy of AAV8-mediated gene therapy (GNT0003) in patients with Crigler-Najjar syndrome, an extremely rare congenital liver disorder affecting approximately 500 people in Europe. It is caused by a deficiency of UGT1A1, an enzyme required for bilirubin metabolism. The accumulation of this substance can lead to irreversible neurological damage and, in the most severe cases, death.
To date, patients have relied on blue-light phototherapy to control their bilirubin levels. Liver transplantation is the only definitive curative treatment option, but it carries a risk of complications. GNT 0003 is a gene therapy aiming to restore UGT1A1 expression in the liver and correct bilirubin levels in patients.
Benefits persist four years after treatment
Lorenzo D'Antiga, director of the pediatrics department at Papa Giovanni XXIII Hospital, and his co-authors documented the persistence of treatment benefits four years after administration in the three patients who received the therapeutic dose at the hospital in Bergamo, Italy. Two of them were able to discontinue phototherapy, while the third maintained a partial response, requiring lower exposure to phototherapy. In all three patients, bilirubin levels remained significantly below the threshold associated with the risk of neurotoxicity.
The investigators also observed a sustained normalization of levels of alanine aminotransferase (ALT), a liver enzyme that is a key marker of liver health and function, in the three patients treated at the highest dose, an effect that had never been achieved with phototherapy alone.
One of the patients also successfully completed a pregnancy without complications following gene therapy and gave birth to a healthy baby.
Testing efficacy in a larger population
This latest publication follows the results of the Phase I–II CureCN trial, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2023. Those results demonstrated the safety of the treatment and its ability to correct the disease, enabling patients who received the therapeutic dose to discontinue phototherapy.
The pivotal part of the trial, which began in January 2023, aims to confirm the observed effect in a larger patient population, including children age 10 and older, as this is the age at which the liver reaches maturity.
Potential beyond Crigler-Najjar syndrome
"The results of this clinical trial open a new path toward the correction of genetic liver diseases that affect both children and adults and would otherwise be incurable," says D'Antiga, director of the pediatrics department at Papa Giovanni XXIII Hospital and principal investigator of the study.
"Until now, adeno-associated virus (AAV) vector gene therapy has shown clinical efficacy in patients with hemophilia A and B. There is now also a clear signal of its efficacy in Crigler–Najjar syndrome. Offering real hope of a cure to patients with severe rare diseases is the greatest reward for physicians and researchers in this field.
"At Papa Giovanni XXIII Hospital in Bergamo, we continue our commitment to clinical research with passion and dedication, bringing to the bedside innovative therapies that may one day be available to all patients with diseases that currently lack a definitive treatment."
"These four-year follow-up results confirm the potential of GNT0003 to change the management of Crigler-Najjar syndrome in the long term. They confirm not only the safety of our approach but, above all, its potential for sustained efficacy over time," says Giuseppe Ronzitti, from Généthon's Immunology and Gene Therapy for Liver Diseases team.
"The teams at Genethon have devoted considerable effort to this project, from initial design of the treatment to clinical trial, and we are very happy with these results, which pave the way for the treatment of other metabolic diseases. This study and those to come also reflect our long-term commitment to finding therapeutic solutions for rare and ultra-rare diseases."
Publication details
Lorenzo D'Antiga et al., Durability of Gene Therapy in Patients with Crigler–Najjar Syndrome, New England Journal of Medicine (2026). DOI: 10.1056/nejmc2603129
Journal information: New England Journal of Medicine

candidato.titulo: Technique that spots tRNAs in action could accelerate drug development for inherited diseases
candidato.resumo: Human cells turn genetic instructions into proteins with great precision. Critical for the translation of this information are transfer RNAs, or tRNAs, small molecules that read the genetic code three letters at a time and bring the matching building blocks of proteins, the amino acids, to the cell's protein-making machinery, the ribosome.

texto_fonte:
Technique that spots tRNAs in action could accelerate drug development for inherited diseases
Human cells turn genetic instructions into proteins with great precision. Critical for the translation of this information are transfer RNAs, or tRNAs, small molecules that read the genetic code three letters at a time and bring the matching building blocks of proteins, the amino acids, to the cell's protein-making machinery, the ribosome.
Every cell holds millions of tRNAs, but only some are busy at work in the ribosome. Until now, scientists have studied them by measuring all of the tRNAs in a cell at once, assuming this gives a fair picture of the ones actually doing the job.
In a new study in Nature Methods, researchers at the Center for Genomic Regulation (CRG) in Barcelona describe a technique that looks only at the tRNAs on ribosomes busy making proteins. It shows that the tRNAs at work can differ from the cell's overall stock, particularly when cells are under stress, a difference that standard techniques miss.
"The field has largely assumed that sequencing all the tRNAs in a cell gives a good picture of the ones working in protein production. Our work shows that this is not necessarily the case, particularly under stress," said Dr. Mie Monti, the study's first author.
Stress reveals an unexpected tRNA buildup
When cells were starved of leucine, one of the building blocks of protein, the team saw the tRNAs piling up on the ribosome, when the expectation would be for tRNAs to disappear entirely.
The results suggest some changes inside cells may have gone unnoticed. Cancer cells, for example, are known to use tRNAs differently from healthy cells, but Monti says this had only been studied by counting every tRNA in the cell.
Human cells also carry several versions of many tRNAs. Using viral infections as an example, Monti says the new approach could show exactly which tRNA molecule a virus relies on. In principle, that could point to new ways of blocking an infection.
Reading past disease-causing stop signals
The biggest implication of the study is that it might accelerate the development of a new kind of medicine for genetic diseases.
About one in 10 of the genetic errors known to cause inherited disease is a typo that tells the cell to stop making a protein too early. Specially designed tRNAs can read past the false stop sign and restore the full protein without changing a patient's DNA.
Experimental tRNA medicines have already restored missing proteins in cells and mice in studies of cystic fibrosis and Duchenne muscular dystrophy, and one was cleared this year for its first trial in people. Because the same typo can appear in many different genes, one tRNA medicine could in theory treat many unrelated conditions.
"A single tRNA medicine could, in principle, be used to treat multiple unrelated rare diseases. This would be transformative for rare disease patients, as these groups are otherwise too fragmented for conventional drug development," says ICREA research professor Eva Novoa, who led the study.
The method could also help those designing such medicines. "One thing is to design a tRNA that works in a test tube. Another is to know that it will actually go to the ribosome in sufficient amounts to be used by the cell," explains Monti.
A faster view of working tRNAs
The authors of the study expect their new method, called tRIBO-seq, will become a routine tool for finding the most promising candidate medicines. The team developed it with the Italian company IMMAGINA Biotechnology.
The method works by fishing for ribosomes that are busy making proteins in a cell. The tRNAs inside are then read one by one, showing which are in use, which chemical tags they carry and whether any are damaged, all in a single experiment.
Conventional methods require about a week of growing cells and need specialist equipment. The CRG's method needs a single dish of cells and about a day and a half.
Publication details
Mie Monti et al., Selective profiling of translationally active tRNAs and their dynamics under stress, Nature Methods (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41592-026-03277-6

candidato.titulo: How did Agility Robotics perform on its first day on the stock market?
candidato.resumo: Humanoid developer Agility Robotics ended its first day of trading on the Nasdaq just 2% above where it started, at $11.49. The post How did Agility Robotics perform on its first day on the stock market? appeared first on The Robot Report .

texto_fonte:
Earlier today, Agility Robotics began trading on the Nasdaq Stock Market under the ticker “AGLT.” The company claimed that it is “the first pure-play legged humanoid company to go public.”
Agility started the day trading at $11.26 per share, above the initial $10 per share price used in the SPAC deal. It was a day of ups and downs, as it was for many tech stocks. It hit its lowest price at $8.40, and its highest at $12.15.
The company ended up closing the day trading slightly above (2%) where it had started, at $11.49. Other pure-play robotics providers did not fare so well.
Serve Robotics, another publicly traded robotics company that offers sidewalk delivery robots, ended down 12.45%. Surgical robotics leader Intuitive Surgical ended down 2.82%. Symbotic, which provides end-to-end warehouse automation, ended down 2.47%. In addition, PROCEPT BioRobotics Corp., which provides robotic aquablation therapy, ended down 6.42%.
While Unitree, another humanoid robotics provider, doesn’t trade on the Nasdaq, it is public on the Shanghai Stock Exchange’s STR Market. It’s one of the only other publicly traded humanoid robot providers.
Unitree first debuted on the market at 150.80 yuan ($22.55 U.S.), and saw some quick success, hitting a high of 1,100 yuan ($164.46) that day. Just a few weeks after debuting on the market, it was down almost 53% from its first-day high. The company is still working to climb back up to those numbers.
In addition, China has reportedly tightened its own requirements for initial public offerings for humanoid robot startups.
Technology and AI-related stocks struggle across markets
Note that the entire Nasdaq is down 5.52% today, which means Agility was beating this overall trend. Much of these losses were concentrated in AI-related stocks.
NVIDIA ended the day down 9.26% from its opening price. AMD ended down 17.26%, while Qualcomm dropped 9.49%. Microsoft was down 3.58%. Rockwell Automation was down 14.15%.
Other markets have had some of their worst days since April 2025. The S&P 500 dropped 4.36%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 3.44%.
This week’s midterm elections have caused the markets to fluctuate. While they saw some sharp gains yesterday, many of those gains dissipated today. Today’s losses have a lot to do with investor uncertainty around future data center buildouts with a now Democratically controlled Senate and House.
What comes next for Agility Robotics
The Robot Report will be watching Agility’s performance on the markets in the coming months. Already, the company alluded to adding more robots to its portfolio. The Robot Report also broke the news about Agility exploring wheel-based robots in September 2026.
Peggy Johnson, Agility’s CEO, talked more about this plan in a recent video. In the video, she mentioned the possible addition of a smaller bipedal form factor to the company’s lineup.
Agility claimed that for its newest Digit 5, it has more than $300 million in committed multiyear orders, subject to contractual milestones and product specifications. It expects to begin Digit 5 deliveries to early-access customers in 2027.
Agility’s public offering, which it conducted after completing a merger with special-purpose acquisition company (SPAC) Churchill Capital Corp XI, will provide around $465 million in gross proceeds before expenses.

candidato.titulo: Yelp Combines Native and Server-Driven UI for Its AI Assistant
candidato.resumo: Yelp combines native mobile controls with server-driven conversation rendering in its AI Assistant using the CHAOS framework. The architecture separates view configuration from conversation data, supports backend-driven chat interactions, and enables faster UI updates without new app releases. Yelp also discusses cross-platform challenges and reuse for its Biz Ask Anything pilot. By Leela Kumili

texto_fonte:
Yelp has adopted a hybrid user interface architecture for its AI Assistant, combining native mobile controls with server-driven conversation rendering to support faster interface changes across platforms. The design uses Yelp’s CHAOS framework, short for Content Hosting Architecture with Optimization Strategies, to render conversation content while keeping navigation and message input native.
Yelp Assistant launched on iOS in 2024 to help users create project requests for local service professionals. It has since expanded to answer questions about businesses and support actions such as reservations, appointments, and food orders.
CHAOS supports web, iOS, and Android. In a server-driven UI architecture, the backend defines what the client displays and how it responds to interactions, so interface changes can reach users without requiring a new mobile app release.
Daniel Andrade Groppe, Services Tech Lead at Yelp, highlighted,
Our existing CHAOS framework lacked some of the capabilities the Assistant required, including text input fields and network requests. Extending the framework would have delayed delivery, so we took a hybrid approach: we kept navigation and message input native while using CHAOS to render the conversation area.
Yelp Assistant UI: Native and Server-Driven Components (Source: Yelp Blog Post)
The implementation separates view configuration from conversation data. When a chat starts, the client fetches the CHAOS configuration and initializes a dataset for message events. Subsequent events update the existing view without refetching the configuration. Events represent persistent user and bot messages, temporary typing indicators and quick replies, and links that open destinations. The backend can also send actions to control the interface. For example, when a project request is complete, it can return a message, a link to view matches, and an action that disables chat input. This event-driven design decouples rendering from conversation logic.
Airbnb has documented a related approach through its Ghost Platform, which uses server-defined UI across web and mobile clients. Both approaches let teams update supported presentation without requiring every change to ship in a new client release. Yelp’s implementation applies this model to a conversational interface while retaining native controls and client-side handling for message state and interactions.
Yelp Assistant UI Chat Interaction Flow (Source: Yelp Blog Post)
The client displays submitted messages and a typing indicator, disables input, and sends requests to the backend. On response, it displays the reply and quick replies and re-enables input. Recoverable errors trigger retries, while non-recoverable failures disable input and prompt users to try again later.
Yelp engineers note that the architecture also introduces coordination challenges and engineers needed time to learn both the Assistant and CHAOS, and shared implementations can still behave differently across platforms. Separating view configuration from conversation data enables independent feature development. The architecture also supported reusing the Android Assistant to launch the Biz Ask Anything pilot. According to Yelp, this work laid the groundwork for its next-generation Assistant, which now connects business information with actions users can take.

candidato.titulo: Nvidia tightens tracking of AI GPUs in Southeast Asia as Chinese chip smuggling draws scrutiny, report claims
candidato.resumo: Nvidia is requiring Southeast Asian cloud providers seeking Nvidia Cloud Partner status to enroll in its Fleet Intelligence tracking program, giving the chipmaker greater visibility into where its AI GPUs are deployed. The move comes as Washington increases pressure over suspected chip smuggling into China, with investigations involving Megaspeed International and Super Micro highlighting the challenges of enforcing U.S. export restrictions

texto_fonte:
Southeast Asia computing providers are now reportedly required to register with Nvidia's Fleet Intelligence tracking system if they want to become official Nvidia Cloud Partners (NCPs). The move, according to Bloomberg, is aimed at giving the chipmaker another way to monitor where its AI accelerators are deployed, as Washington grows increasingly frustrated with restricted hardware finding its way into China through regional smuggling networks. Nvidia was not immediately available for comment.
The NCP designation is worth pursuing as it gives cloud providers Nvidia's public endorsement and preferred access to its sought-after AI chips, putting the company in a position to use those benefits as leverage. Customers seeking the status must now enroll in Fleet Intelligence, according to people familiar with the new requirements. Fleet Management was introduced last December primarily as a data centre management tool. It gathers information about NVIDIA hardware deployed across participating companies' infrastructure, including the locations of individual accelerators. That information could give Nvidia a better picture of whether its chips are operating after they leave the supply chain.
The system is, however, a universal tracking mandate. Participation has remained voluntary outside the NCP requirement, and Nvidia does not automatically receive location data from every customer using the software. The company has also not clarified whether existing Cloud Partners will have to enroll to retain their designation or whether the requirement will eventually extend beyond Southeast Asia.
Notably, Nvidia has been developing a way to locate AI for some time now. Last December, we reported that the company had developed software-based GPU tracking, using GPU telemetry and network latency measurements to estimate where processors are operating. Nvidia described the software as a customer-installed agent for monitoring hardware health, integrity and inventory.
The technology has an obvious use beyond data maintenance. The U.S. restricts Chinese companies from purchasing advanced AI accelerators without a license, yet authorities believe billions of dollars worth of the hardware have reached Chinese buyers through third-party networks, with Southeast Asia becoming an important transit point for those transactions.
A C4ADS investigation has previously identified several routes used to move restricted processors into China, including purchases through research initiatives, shell companies and shipments routed through other Southeast Asian countries. The nonprofit examined transactions between 2022 and 2025 and identified $13.4 million worth of Nvidia A100, H100, and AD102-series GPUs moving through regional trade routes. Its report also linked $4.6 billion in hardware purchases to Singapore-based Megaspeed International.
Megaspeed has become a particularly awkward case for Nvidia, with the company being under U.S. and Singaporean investigation for more than a year over suspected chip diversion. Last week, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang defended his dealings with the firm, describing them as “completely normal,” adding, “we’ve studied all their deployments of our GPUs and counted every one.” Megaspeed denied any wrongdoing. In April, Megaspeed’s Malysisan data centre landlord terminated its contract, reallocating 68.4 megawatts of capacity to another cloud provider
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Moreover, Megaspeed is not the only example of how difficult it can be to police the movement of AI hardware. Earlier this year, U.S. prosecutors accused people associated with Super Micro of helping divert around $2.5 billion worth of Nvidia-powered servers to China through Southeast Asian intermediaries. The alleged scheme involved falsified paperwork and dummy server shells, with genuine hardware shipped onward after inspections. More recently, the company has faced additional scrutiny over its export compliance after inspections. Nvidia has also reportedly removed half of the Asian companies on its pre-approved buyer list and told cloud providers to keep at least 51% of their computing services with customers outside China.
Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Newton Gitonga is a tech journalist covering gadgets, PC hardware, AI, data centers, and the wider tech industry. His interest in technology started early, taking apart things around the house to see how they worked, often to his dad’s frustration. His curiosity sometimes got the better of him, including a few failed attempts to fix laptops, one of them a gifted Dell XPS. He has previously written for Notebookcheck, ZyCrypto, CoinCentral, and Crypto News Flash.

candidato.titulo: NASA’s Swift telescope falls to Earth after nearly 22 years in space
candidato.resumo: After nearly 22 years of exploring the universe’s most violent explosions, NASA’s Swift Observatory has re-entered Earth’s atmosphere over Indonesia. Originally designed to last just two years, the pioneering space telescope transformed our understanding of black holes, exploding stars, and mysterious cosmic outbursts.

texto_fonte:
NASAâs Swift telescope falls to Earth after nearly 22 years in space
- Date:
- November 6, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- After nearly 22 years of exploring the universeâs most violent explosions, NASAâs Swift Observatory has re-entered Earthâs atmosphere over Indonesia. Originally designed to last just two years, the pioneering space telescope transformed our understanding of black holes, exploding stars, and mysterious cosmic outbursts.
- Share:
NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory has returned to Earth after spending nearly 22 years in space, bringing an extraordinary era of astronomical discovery to a close. The spacecraft re-entered Earth's atmosphere on Wednesday, ending a mission that lasted more than ten times longer than originally planned.
Launched in 2004, Swift was a pioneering space observatory equipped with three telescopes designed to study some of the most powerful explosions in the universe. Its instruments could detect different types of light, allowing scientists to investigate energetic cosmic events that would be difficult to understand using a single telescope.
NASA's Swift Observatory Re-Enters Earth's Atmosphere
The U.S. Space Force confirmed that Swift entered the atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST on Wednesday above North Sumatra, Indonesia. The reported location was approximately 3.4 degrees north latitude and 98.6 degrees east longitude.
NASA anticipated that most of the spacecraft would burn up as it plunged through the atmosphere. However, officials acknowledged that some components might have survived the intense heat of re-entry.
A Two-Year NASA Mission That Lasted Nearly 22 Years
Swift was originally developed to investigate gamma-ray bursts, extraordinarily powerful flashes of high-energy radiation associated with some of the most extreme events in the cosmos. These bursts can occur when massive stars collapse or when certain compact objects, such as neutron stars, merge.
Although NASA initially planned for Swift to operate for just two years, the observatory continued making scientific contributions for more than two decades.
One of its most important capabilities was its ability to respond quickly to sudden cosmic events. When Swift detected an energetic outburst, it could rapidly redirect its telescopes toward the source and notify observatories around the world. This coordinated approach allowed astronomers to study brief astronomical phenomena before they faded from view.
Swift also observed multiple wavelengths of light, giving researchers different ways to examine the same event and better understand the physical processes behind it.
From Black Holes to Exploding Stars
Over its remarkably long lifetime, Swift's scientific contributions expanded far beyond its original focus on gamma-ray bursts.
The observatory helped astronomers investigate active galaxies powered by supermassive black holes, stars that produce powerful X-ray flares, and supernovae, the enormous explosions that mark the deaths of certain stars.
Its observations also extended much closer to home, including studies of comets and asteroids within our own solar system.
By combining rapid observations with the ability to detect different forms of radiation, Swift became a valuable tool for exploring both distant cosmic explosions and nearby objects. Its re-entry marks the end of a mission that greatly exceeded its planned lifespan and helped transform scientists' understanding of some of the universe's most energetic phenomena.

candidato.titulo: Study Maps 24 Problems Where Quantum Computers Could Gain an Edge
candidato.resumo: Insider Brief Quantum computers could deliver substantial speedups on 24 computational problems, but a new study also reveals the challenging conditions that would make those gains useful. Researchers affiliated with the Open Quantum Institute, hosted at CERN, Google Quantum AI, Microsoft, Oratomic, NVIDIA, JPMorganChase, MIT, Harvard University and other institutions have assembled a guide to […]

texto_fonte:
Insider Brief
- Researchers identified 24 computational problems with potential for substantial quantum speedups and outlined the conditions needed to achieve them.
- The study covers areas including chemistry, optimization and data analysis, connecting theoretical quantum methods with possible practical applications.
- Preparing data, correcting errors and reading results can erase potential gains, requiring researchers to assess the full calculation against leading classical methods.
Quantum computers could deliver substantial speedups on 24 computational problems, but a new study also reveals the challenging conditions that would make those gains useful.
Researchers affiliated with the Open Quantum Institute, hosted at CERN, Google Quantum AI, Microsoft, Oratomic, NVIDIA, JPMorganChase, MIT, Harvard University and other institutions have assembled a guide to problems with credible prospects for quantum advantage — or, the ability for quantum machines to outperform classical computing methods.
For each problem, the researchers describe the mathematical structure, data requirements and other conditions needed to preserve a quantum computer’s potential edge. The aim is to help scientists and industry specialists identify where theoretical gains could translate into practical applications.
The paper, which was posted to the preprint server arXiv, is a synthesis of existing research. It cautions that a theoretical speed advantage does not guarantee faster results in practice. A quantum algorithm may require far fewer steps than a classical method on large problems, yet still take longer to produce a useful answer. Preparing data, correcting errors and reading the results can erase the expected time savings, the researchers write.
The collection spans number theory, optimization, statistical inference, quantum simulation, linear algebra and the analysis of shapes and connections in data. Potential applications include chemistry, materials research, signal processing and code breaking, although the evidence and maturity vary substantially across entries.
A Higher Bar for Advantage
The researchers focus on speedups greater than quadratic, a threshold they argue will likely be needed to overcome the substantial operating costs of early quantum computers equipped with error correction.
A quadratic speedup means that if a classical computer needs roughly 1 million steps, a quantum algorithm might need about 1,000. That does not necessarily mean it finishes 1,000 times faster, because each quantum step can take more time and resources
The compendium instead includes stronger improvements, ranging from cubic and quartic gains to exponential separations. These describe how the work required grows as problems get larger, rather than how many times faster a quantum computer would be on every calculation.
The comparisons are generally against the best classical methods currently known. The team stresses that those methods can improve and an advantage over today’s leading classical algorithm does not necessarily prove that no better classical approach exists.
The study also distinguishes several kinds of evidence, including rigorous mathematical results, evidence limited to particular classes of classical methods, and numerical or heuristic studies. Its maximum-speedup labels describe the strongest result identified under specified conditions, rather than a promise for every instance of a problem.
The researchers favor starting with computational tasks for which quantum advantages are already supported, then looking for real problems that fit their requirements. Starting with a pressing business or scientific challenge and searching for a quantum solution is often unsuccessful because useful quantum algorithms depend on mathematical structures that many problems lack.
Where the Conditions Matter
Solving systems of linear equations — sets of equations that describe relationships among quantities, such as currents in an electrical circuit — shows how large potential quantum speed gains can depend on strict conditions.
These equations appear throughout science and engineering, such as calculating forces on bridges, analyzing currents in electrical circuits and modeling heat flowing through materials. The study indicates that quantum algorithms can offer exponential improvements in some settings, but the numbers that define the equations must be organized in ways that a quantum computer can load quickly. The equations must also be solvable without numerical difficulties that slow the calculation.
The output is another constraint. A quantum computer also stores the answer in a form that must be measured to obtain usable numbers. For example, an engineer modeling heat flow might need a broad measure of how heat spreads, rather than the temperature at every point in a material. Quantum methods are better suited to extracting a few such measures; retrieving every temperature value could erase the time savings, according to the study.
The researchers detailed a similar problem with loading arbitrary data. If preparing the input requires work proportional to the dataset’s size, an apparent exponential improvement in the central calculation may disappear, according to the paper.
In chemistry, the study examines how quantum computers could calculate a molecule’s lowest possible energy, known as its ground-state energy. This helps researchers determine how its atoms arrange themselves and how it might react with other molecules — information useful for developing battery materials or substances that capture carbon dioxide.
The study suggests three criteria for producing practical quantum advantage. First, the system must fit within available computing resources. Researchers must also be able to prepare a suitable initial quantum state. Finally, the chosen problem must resist efficient classical methods, the researchers write.
The study identifies preparing those initial states and establishing which scientifically relevant systems are consistently difficult for classical computers as important unresolved challenges. It places the ground-state energy result it reviews in its earlier research category, while noting that more advanced work on the same broader problem may exist outside the entry’s scope.
Another example involves finding patterns buried in noisy data, such as measurements with random errors. The study describes a quantum method that could sharply reduce the work needed to uncover certain patterns as datasets grow larger, though the advantage depends on specific conditions.
That improvement applies within a particular range of signal strength and problem structure. It does not extend to ordinary matrix principal component analysis, which already has efficient classical methods. Showing that similar gains survive in messier datasets, including sparse or contaminated data, remains a research task, according to the study.
Even a candidate with evidence of favorable scaling may require formidable hardware. For a specific random constraint-satisfaction problem, the paper cites an analysis placing the quantum-classical crossover at approximately 15 hours using roughly 74 million physical qubits, under the assumed error rate and error-correction design. The estimate illustrates the distance that can separate a mathematical advantage from an affordable computation.
From Candidate Problems to Useful Work
The researchers group the 24 computational problems identified in the study into two stages based on how much is known about their potential quantum advantage.
Stage I includes tasks where research suggests quantum computers could have an edge, but scientists still need to identify specific examples where that advantage would hold. Stage II goes further, identifying examples they can readily construct that quantum computers are expected to solve faster than the best available classical methods and machines.
The next step is showing that those examples address a useful scientific or technological question. Simulating a molecule faster, for instance, matters only if the result helps researchers understand its behavior or develop a new material, according to the study.
Each of the 24 entries explains the problem, where it might be useful, how quantum and classical methods compare, and what conditions are needed for a quantum advantage. The guide is aimed at scientists and other specialists who understand computing but may not know how to apply quantum methods to their work.
Researchers must also be able to check whether an answer is reliable. Depending on the problem, that could involve checking it with a classical computer, running another quantum calculation or comparing the result with a physical experiment.
Much of the remaining work involves making the full calculation more efficient, from preparing the information a quantum computer needs to reading its answer. Researchers must also test whether the methods work on a wider range of problems and retain their advantage as classical computing methods improve.
The guide’s 24 entries give researchers a starting point: problems where quantum computers could offer substantial gains, the conditions those gains depend on and the questions that remain before they can be put to practical use.
The research team included Philipp Kammerlander of the Open Quantum Institute; Thomas E. O’Brien, Robbie King, Rolando D. Somma, Mária Kieferová, Alexander Schmidhuber, Siddhartha Jain, Andi Gu, Guang Hao Low, Dar Gilboa and Ryan Babbush of Google Quantum AI; Brad Lackey and Matthias Troyer of Microsoft; Yuri Alexeev and Elica Kyoseva of NVIDIA; Shouvanik Chakrabarti and Ruslan Shaydulin of JPMorganChase; Pietro M. Posta and Matthias Christandl of the University of Copenhagen; Barry C. Sanders of the University of Calgary; and Catherine Lefebvre of the Geneva Science and Diplomacy Anticipator.
For a deeper, more technical dive, please review the paper on arXiv. It’s important to note that arXiv is a pre-print server, which allows researchers to receive quick feedback on their work. However, it is not — nor is this article, itself — official peer-review publications. Peer-review is an important step in the scientific process to verify results.

texto_fonte:
Valve spent the last decade making Windows optional for PC gaming. Now it wants to do the same thing to x86 — the Intel- and AMD-based CPU architecture at the heart of every gaming PC. If it succeeds, the resulting shake-up could change what “PC game” even means.
The Steam Deck proved Valve’s Proton compatibility layer could run an enormous library of Windows games on Linux without developers needing to port them to Linux first. That breakthrough helped make the Steam Deck a success. It also made Linux gaming legitimately viable, and laid the groundwork for SteamOS to spread to other PCs.
But the Steam Frame reveals that Valve’s ambitions go much deeper. The standalone VR headset runs SteamOS on a Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen 3 processor based on the Arm architecture, rather than the x86 processors from AMD and Intel that have powered PC gaming for decades.
And Valve expects your existing x86 Windows games to run on it anyway. That’s why the Arm chip inside Steam Frame matters so much more than VR. Valve is starting to dismantle the fundamental assumptions about which hardware and software a gaming PC needs to run your games.
The writing is on the wall. We’re looking at the endgame for everything Valve has been building with SteamOS, Proton, Steam Deck, and now Steam Frame: Buy anywhere, play anywhere. Your Steam library won’t care what operating system you’re using, what processor architecture sits inside your device, or, eventually, even what type of device you’re holding. As long as you’ve got enough compute and graphics horsepower to run the game, Steam will figure out the rest.
And that would be a true game-changer. Buckle up.
Hi! I’m Brad, PCWorld’s executive editor. Want to get more hard-hitting journalism like this wherever you are? Sign up for PCWorld’s Full Nerd and Boost Mode newsletters for PC enthusiasts, and be sure to subscribe to PCWorld on YouTube and all the usual social channels. Welcome to the PCWorld family!
First Valve made Windows optional
The Steam Deck’s software magic is easy to take for granted now, but it’s worth revisiting how crazy its basic premise once sounded.
Most PC games are Windows games. Valve didn’t solve that problem by convincing thousands of developers to create and maintain native Linux versions. It built Proton to let the Windows versions run on Linux instead.
There’s a lot happening under Proton’s hood. It’s built around Wine, while components like DXVK translate DirectX graphics calls into Vulkan. The important bit is that all this happens underneath the game. Developers can keep shipping Windows games. Gamers can keep buying Windows games. Valve resolves the incompatibility.
That strategy didn’t start with Steam Deck. Valve’s push toward Linux began in earnest during the Windows 8 era, when Microsoft’s Windows Store and its increasingly locked-down approach to computing convinced Gabe Newell that Valve needed an escape hatch. The original SteamOS and Steam Machines last decade were that hedge. They failed as products, but Valve never abandoned the underlying work.
Proton eventually attacked the fatal chicken-and-egg problem that helped doom Steam Machines: Gamers wouldn’t switch to Linux because their Windows games weren’t there, while developers wouldn’t support Linux because the gamers weren’t there.
So Valve stopped asking developers to port their games.
Instead of demanding that the PC gaming ecosystem bend around SteamOS, Valve bent SteamOS around the PC gaming ecosystem. Steam Deck was the culmination of that decade-long push toward independence.
Willis Lai/Foundry
Omdia analyst James McWhirter traces Valve’s strategy back to exactly the same place. “The very first 2013 release of SteamOS and Steam Machines were a hedge against Windows 8 sidelining the old Win32 framework by which so many games depended on,” McWhirter told me via email.
Much has changed since then, he said, but “the spirit of SteamOS, giving Valve more control of its own destiny, has remained a key constant.” And now Steam Frame takes the same idea one layer deeper.
Now Valve is making x86 optional
Steam Frame doesn’t just have an operating-system compatibility problem. Its Snapdragon processor speaks a fundamentally different language than the x86 code compiled for traditional gaming PCs.
That’s where FEX comes in.
Valve
FEX translates x86 code into Arm64 instructions that the Snapdragon processor can understand. Stack it together with Proton and something kind of bonkers becomes possible: You can take an x86 game compiled for Windows and run it on an Arm processor running Linux.
But Valve isn’t simply emulating an entire x86 Windows PC and hoping for the best. “When provided with a proper ARM execution environment, such as when integrated with Proton ARM, FEX only translates the CPU code of the application,” Valve software engineer Pierre-Loup Griffais told me via email.
That’s a crucial distinction. Proton itself, the operating system, and graphics drivers can execute natively on Arm. Griffais says Proton crosses over at the Win32 API boundary, meaning “no Proton, OS or graphics driver code requires translation.” FEX primarily has to deal with the game’s own CPU code.
“The FEX translation overhead is only on the game’s own CPU code and is typically pretty modest,” Griffais said. “For a typical GPU-bound game, our aim is that the output performance would be similar to running the game on a similarly powerful GPU without CPU translation.”
Foundry
That’s the technical detail that makes the bigger idea possible. Valve hasn’t made processor architecture irrelevant. It’s trying to turn architecture from a compatibility veto into a performance tradeoff.
That’s essentially the same trick Proton pulled on Windows. Valve doesn’t need the underlying technology to disappear. It just needs it to stop being something that can dictate where your Steam library runs.
Griffais says that if an Arm chip offers enough of a performance-per-watt advantage at a given power envelope, it could become a viable SteamOS gaming chip “even with FEX translation overhead in the picture.” There are still catches, which we’ll get to later. But those catches are increasingly questions about how well a game runs rather than whether x86 Windows software can run at all.
Valve has been here before
Getting software to technically run isn’t enough. Translation has to feel invisible, too.
“FEX code caching is vital for frame time consistency,” Griffais said, and Valve plans to integrate it with Steam Pre-Caching so translated code can eventually be ready before you launch a game. It’s the sort of deeply boring engineering work that separates getting Doom to boot on a weird processor from making translated games actually feel native.
And Valve has been doing that work for a long time.
For FEX, Griffais said, the challenge was getting it ready to run modern games with minimal performance loss. “It’s a fairly binary threshold to hit, but it took nearly a decade to get there,” he said.
Meanwhile, Arm chips were becoming faster and adding CPU and GPU features better suited to PC gaming. Valve’s early FEX work helped inform that process through conversations with chip vendors about what Valve wanted from the hardware.
“Timing-wise, FEX readiness and availability of ARM chips powerful enough to play the latest PC games ended up hitting at around the same time,” Griffais said.
We’ve seen this movie before. Proton took years of mostly invisible compatibility work before Valve could build a Steam Deck around it. FEX followed a remarkably similar path before surfacing inside Steam Frame. Valve keeps doing the hard compatibility work first, then building new hardware around the freedom it creates.
Don’t port your game. Steam will figure it out
All this compatibility work raises an obvious question: What does Valve actually want game developers to do about this new world of Windows, Linux, x86, Arm, and Android?
Not much, actually. Valve’s guidance to developers is revealing.
Steam Frame can run native Arm Linux software. Valve also created Lepton, a containerized compatibility layer for Android games. But for most PC developers, Valve isn’t asking for another bespoke version of their game. 
Valve
Valve says most developers can support Steam Frame by simply running their existing Windows x86 version through Proton and FEX. Proton handles Windows. FEX handles x86. SteamOS handles the rest.
Steam Frame can therefore accommodate Windows x86 games through Proton and FEX, Linux x86 games through FEX, Android Arm software through Lepton, and native Arm software directly. That’s the bigger point: SteamOS is increasingly becoming an abstraction layer between the games in your Steam library and whatever hardware happens to sit underneath it.
Valve isn’t betting that Arm replaces x86 or Linux replaces Windows. It’s building Steam so it doesn’t have to care what replaces what. You can just play your games.
Proton didn’t require Windows to lose. It made Windows less important to Valve. FEX doesn’t require x86 to lose. It just makes x86 less important to Valve.
Arm could change what a Steam PC looks like
Arm is the big wildcard, and that’s where hardware possibilities get interesting. The interesting part isn’t merely swapping one CPU architecture for another. It’s what becomes possible if Arm’s performance-per-watt strengths survive the translation layer.
Hannah Cowton-Barnes / Foundry
McWhirter points to Nintendo’s Switch 2. The system’s Nvidia Arm SoC consumes around 6 watts in handheld mode, with total system power around 10 watts, while AI technologies like DLSS help it deliver graphical fidelity far beyond what those power figures might suggest.
PC handhelds generally live much higher on the power curve, often around 15 to 35 watts. That means bigger batteries, more cooling, more weight, and thicker devices.
Arm doesn’t automatically fix that, and Steam Frame certainly doesn’t prove it will. But if FEX makes translation cheap enough while Arm silicon provides a meaningful efficiency advantage, the design space for SteamOS hardware gets a lot more interesting.
“The result is we’ll see more form factors unlocked for SteamOS devices,” McWhirter said.
Handhelds are obvious SteamOS targets, but so are laptops, mini PCs, living-room boxes, and maybe even devices we haven’t even considered yet. Qualcomm’s involvement matters beyond its processor, too: McWhirter notes that the company is contributing to the open-source Mesa graphics stack, attacking another major barrier to Arm PC gaming.
Mark Hachman / Foundry
Valve still needs other silicon vendors and PC manufacturers to buy in. McWhirter thinks Nvidia could be a particularly important tipping point, and the recent debut of RTX Spark laptops shows its interest in this space. And Arm systems won’t get a free pass simply for being efficient; they still need to compete against increasingly potent x86 hardware on performance, price, and margins.
But that’s the whole point. If Valve’s compatibility work succeeds, Arm versus x86 becomes a hardware competition rather than a library-compatibility decision.
That’s great news for gamers. Once processor architecture stops dictating which games you can play, chipmakers have to compete on performance, battery life, thermals, form factor, and price. Arm won’t automatically deliver better gaming PCs, but giving manufacturers more viable hardware choices should put some welcome pressure on AMD and Intel, too.
Steam Deck helps from the other direction
FEX can’t magically make an underpowered GPU run a game that needs dramatically more horsepower. Fortunately for Valve, PC games are already becoming accustomed to scaling down.
Steam Deck contributes to that. Omdia’s 2026 Game Developer Collective survey found 34 percent of developers said handheld gaming PCs have had a major or minor influence on their games’ design. Developers routinely optimize around the Deck, and some games ship with dedicated Deck presets.
My first instinct was to see a Valve-specific flywheel here: More lower-powered Steam devices give developers more reason to make games scale down; more scalable games make more lower-powered Steam hardware viable.
McWhirter thinks that’s overstating Valve’s role, and I think he’s right.
Chris Hoffman / Foundry
Nintendo already spent years convincing publishers to target the modest original Switch. Switch 2 provides another incentive. Digital distribution has also made everything from indies to decade-old games commercially relevant alongside new AAA blockbusters.
But that actually reinforces the broader opportunity for Valve. It doesn’t need every new triple-A game to run beautifully on every conceivable SteamOS device. It simply needs enough of your existing Steam backlog to work.
Steam already contains thousands of excellent games that don’t demand cutting-edge silicon. As that library becomes more portable across operating systems and processor architectures, manufacturers can potentially build Steam devices around different performance targets rather than one ever-escalating definition of a “gaming PC.”
The harder problem may become telling players which games fit which devices—a problem Valve has already started tackling with Deck Verified and Steam Frame’s verification program.
The walls haven’t disappeared
Anti-cheat remains an annoying bastard despite recent improvements.
The software that publishers use to detect and block cheating is deeply intertwined with the operating system, and McWhirter calls it the biggest barrier to SteamOS expanding beyond traditional Windows gaming PCs. Valve has made strides with BattlEye and Easy Anti-Cheat, but publisher-specific systems such as EA’s Javelin and Activision’s Ricochet remain unsupported.
Valve can engineer around Windows APIs and x86 instructions. It can’t unilaterally make somebody else’s anti-cheat stack support an environment they don’t want to support.
Activision
Griffais flags the same issue for Arm. GPUs remain another constraint, as do memory, battery life, price, and plain old horsepower. Software abstraction doesn’t cancel out physics.
Nor does every form factor make sense for every PC game. McWhirter points to triple-A gaming’s struggles on smartphones: controller requirements, limited storage, and games designed for sustained attention don’t disappear merely because the software technically runs. “Play anywhere” doesn’t mean Cyberpunk will run on a toaster.
Buy anywhere, play anywhere
Put all these pieces together and Valve’s trajectory becomes hard to miss.
Steam has always been obsessed with removing friction. Gabe Newell famously argued that piracy was “almost always a service problem and not a pricing problem.” More than two decades later, Valve is applying that same instinct to the boundaries around your game library.
Steam started life as a Windows-based store selling Windows-based games for x86 PCs. Microsoft’s locked-down Windows Store ambitions during the Windows 8 era showed Valve the danger of building that business on assumptions controlled by somebody else. SteamOS gave it an escape hatch. Proton weakened the Windows requirement. Steam Deck proved the approach could underpin an entirely new class of gaming PC. FEX now attacks the x86 requirement. Lepton pulls Android software into the fold.
Every step removes another assumption about what a Steam gaming device needs to be.
Valve doesn’t need SteamOS to replace Windows or Arm to replace x86. Its prize is more fundamental: a Steam library that survives whatever happens underneath it. And that should ultimately be good for us, The Gamers. The best version of this future isn’t one where Arm defeats x86 or SteamOS defeats Windows. It’s one where those choices stop deciding which games you get to play.
That’s why the Arm chip inside Steam Frame matters so much more than VR. Valve isn’t just building another headset. It’s spending years—sometimes a decade at a time—systematically removing dependencies out of Steam itself.
Buy anywhere. Play anywhere. Just bring enough hardware.

O recente aumento significativo no volume e na gravidade dos ataques cibernéticos globais está intimamente associado ao avanço das ferramentas de inteligência artificial, que passam a ser utilizadas por indivíduos mal-intencionados para vasculhar códigos de software e identificar com rapidez fragilidades que permaneceram ocultas por décadas.

Como os atacantes levam vantagem estratégica ao escolher o momento e a vítima, a mitigação desses riscos não depende exclusivamente de soluções tecnológicas, mas de uma governança de segurança robusta e proativa por parte das organizações, prevendo-se uma seleção natural no mercado em que apenas as empresas verdadeiramente resilientes conseguirão manter a confiança de seus usuários.

texto_fonte:
New instrument at Brazil's Sirius accelerator enables researchers to observe solar cells in operation
Scientists at the Brazilian Center for Research in Energy and Materials (CNPEM) in Campinas, São Paulo state, developed an instrument for the Sirius particle accelerator that can observe the interior of solar cells on a nanoscale while they are operating. Rather than analyzing isolated components in a laboratory setting, this new platform enables the evaluation of complete devices generating electricity under real operating conditions. It simulates daily exposure to light, heat and humidity.
The team created a system with high mechanical stability to prevent the samples from shifting out of the X-ray beam's focus, even under extreme temperature fluctuations.
Understanding how the atomic structure and chemistry of these materials react to the environment is essential to investigating the causes of their degradation. This technology will be a crucial tool for optimizing emerging solar technologies, such as perovskite cells, paving the way for cheaper, more efficient and more durable solar energy sources.
"We sought to reproduce the normal operating conditions of the solar cell and use the available techniques at the Sirius accelerator to observe what happens within the material," says Rodrigo Szostak, a researcher at the Brazilian National Synchrotron Light Laboratory (LNLS-CNPEM) and the first author of the study published in the journal Photon Science.
As the researcher explains, X-rays offer a key advantage in this type of research. Due to their penetrating power, X-rays allow for examination of the different layers of the device with minimal sample preparation. This reduces the risk that the experimental procedure itself might alter what is intended to be observed.
The platform was designed primarily for studying perovskite solar cells, a technology that has advanced rapidly in recent years due to the high efficiency of these materials and the ability to manufacture them using simple processes at low temperatures without a vacuum.
Szostak has been following this trajectory since the beginning of his career. He conducted one of the first studies on perovskite solar cells in Brazil.
"These cells have only been in development for about 15 or 20 years, but companies are already beginning to launch commercial products based on them. At the same time, several questions remain unanswered, and the academic community continues to conduct research to understand what's happening," he says.
One of the most important questions concerns stability. While a solar cell is operating, its material is not static. Light, heat, humidity and the electrical voltage itself can cause changes to its structure and composition. Some of these changes are reversible, but others can contribute to the degradation of the device.
"A solar cell undergoes temperature fluctuations every day. As they say in the field, it goes through 'cycling.' We want to understand the effect of these cycles, as well as those caused by light and humidity, on its performance," the researcher points out.
What sets the platform apart is its ability to correlate these macroscopic variables with what occurs on much smaller scales. "We can measure the device's efficiency by varying temperature and humidity while simultaneously using X-ray techniques to examine its chemical composition, physical form, atomic structure and even its electronic structure," Szostak notes.
Achieving this required developing a stable sample holder and a small experimental environment in which the cell can be heated, illuminated, exposed to different atmospheres and electrically connected.
One of the most significant challenges was temperature. To microscopically track the changes caused by heating, the same region of the cell must be observed repeatedly. However, repeated exposure to X-rays can heat, expand and displace the device. Given the scale at which the experiment is conducted, even an almost imperceptible displacement can move the selected region out of the field of view.
"Since we're working with a beam about 200 nanometers wide—hundreds of times thinner than a human hair—we need the sample to remain stationary," Szostak explains. "Our engineering team worked with us to develop a way to secure the sample and accommodate this expansion."
Heating without losing the target
The solution began with the development of a small chip on which the solar cell itself is built. The substrate is a piece of glass coated on one side with indium tin oxide (ITO). This material serves as a transparent, electrically conductive base upon which the solar cell material (perovskite) is built.
On the other side of the glass are two extremely thin platinum circuits: one functions as a heater, and the other as a temperature sensor. Passing current through the first circuit produces heat, and the electrical resistance of the second circuit allows the temperature of the sample to be determined precisely.
"The system concentrates the heating in an area of just 3 by 3 millimeters. The smaller the heated region, the less thermal expansion the experimental setup tends to experience. Tests with an infrared camera showed that the temperature in this small area is quite uniform: at 150 °C, the relative variation was only 0.85 °C," Szostak reports.
The mount itself also required precision engineering solutions. It uses a titanium alloy with low thermal expansion and flexible elements that allow the glass to expand without accumulating stresses that could cause it to break while keeping the cell firmly in place. The system was thermally decoupled from the structures responsible for moving the sample to reduce heat transfer and unwanted displacements.
"That's one of the innovations of this work. We have excellent positional stability. I reviewed the literature, and as far as we know, our holder likely offers the best positional stability ever achieved for this type of experiment," says the researcher.
In tests conducted at Sirius, the sample was repeatedly subjected to temperatures of 30 °C and 150 °C for approximately 20 hours. Over this 120 °C range, the vertical displacement was just 5 micrometers, and the horizontal displacement was about 1 micrometer. More importantly, these displacements were reproducible and reversible. When the temperature returned to its initial value, the sample practically returned to its previous position.
After thermal stabilization, the residual movement was small enough to not cause significant distortions in the images produced during the scans. Temperature control also proved to be fast and precise.
The programmed temperature was reached in less than two minutes, and at 150 °C, it remained stable with general fluctuations of less than 0.1 °C for 50 minutes. The ITO-based chip can be used at temperatures up to 150 °C. In experiments that do not require a conductive substrate, the system can reach 300 °C.
Light, heat and humidity
Temperature is just one of the controlled variables. The device features a small, sealed chamber in which gases can circulate, and humidity levels at the inlet and outlet can be monitored. This allows for the simulation of different atmospheric conditions and investigation of the role of humidity in the degradation of perovskites, for example.
"Another essential component is the lighting. To study a solar cell in operation, it must be illuminated while X-rays take measurements. A xenon lamp would better reproduce all the colors and characteristics of sunlight, but it would be too large for the space available in the experimental station. We therefore opted for a broadband white LED, chosen because, among the LEDs evaluated, it had the spectral distribution closest to sunlight and covered the wavelength range absorbed by the perovskite cell," says Szostak.
The issue of lighting has not yet been fully resolved. When placed directly in front of the cell, the LED can provide an irradiance equivalent to that of the sun, about 100 milliwatts per square centimeter. However, this position blocks certain X-ray transmission geometries.
In the lateral configuration required to allow the beam to pass freely, the intensity reaching the cell corresponds to approximately 30% of the reference solar radiation. Improving this system is among the next steps of the project.
The cell under X-rays
The researchers conducted the experimental demonstration presented in the article with this setup. They fabricated a complete perovskite cell on the chip and subjected it to conventional electrical characterization and various X-ray analyses. The researchers obtained its current-voltage curves and monitored its response when the illumination was turned on and off.
This was made possible thanks to the characteristics of the Carnaúba beamline, one of 12 beamlines installed at the Sirius accelerator. It is designed to perform analyses using an extremely focused X-ray beam.
"The apparatus functions like a multi-technique microscope. We have a very narrow X-ray beam, which allows us to examine the electronic structure, atomic structure and chemical composition of materials in high resolution, in two or three dimensions," Szostak explains.
At the Tarumã station, where the device was installed and which is part of the Carnaúba beamline, different techniques provide complementary information. X-ray diffraction investigates the crystalline structure, X-ray fluorescence maps the distribution of chemical elements, and X-ray absorption spectroscopy provides information on the chemical state of the elements, bond distances and coordination environments.
The station also supports X-ray-excited optical luminescence and other techniques, some of which are still in the implementation phase.
"Basically, the Carnaúba beamline is a super-powerful microscope with which we can examine matter in many different ways," the researcher summarizes. "And its field of application is much broader than that of solar cells: it includes batteries, plants, seeds, biological materials and even paleontological samples."
In the experiment with the perovskite cell, X-ray fluorescence produced maps of the iodine and lead distribution in the device. On the other hand, diffraction made it possible to visualize individual perovskite grains about two micrometers in diameter and to obtain information about their spatial orientation and the exact distance between the atoms in their structure, or the crystal lattice parameters.
These parameters are important because they allow one to estimate material deformations related to properties such as electronic structure, ion migration, defect formation and stability.
To demonstrate this capability, the researchers mapped the crystal structure of the perovskite at 40 °C, then repeated the measurement after raising the temperature to 65 °C.
The expected increase in the lattice parameter, or the characteristic dimension of the crystal structure, could be observed directly. Thus, the sequence of maps revealed not only the microscopic structure of the cell, but also how it transformed in response to a controlled external variable.
"It's precisely this combination that gives the platform its main potential. A single region of the cell can undergo cycles of heating, illumination, humidity or electrical voltage, while different techniques simultaneously or sequentially monitor what happens to its chemical composition, crystal structure and performance. In this way, it'll be possible to investigate the relationships between microscopic changes and the loss—or improvement—of the cell's ability to convert light into electricity," the researcher explains.
The equipment is no longer just an experimental prototype. Developed during Szostak's project, it is now a multi-user facility available to the research community. Several experiments are currently underway.
Although it has been optimized for perovskite solar cells, it can be used for other applications as well. It can also be used to study organic solar cells, solid-state dye-sensitized cells, quantum dot cells, light-emitting diodes (LEDs) and other devices built on compatible substrates.
"Any device or material that can be deposited on glass and that one wishes to study under heating conditions can, in principle, be investigated," the researcher states.
More information
Rodrigo Szostak et al., Visualizing Solar Cells at Work: An in Situ Sample Holder for Multimodal X-ray Nanoscopy under Realistic Operating Conditions, Photon Science (2026). DOI: 10.1021/photonsci.6c00013

texto_fonte:
CISA, FBI, HHS, USDA, and DOT Urge Critical Infrastructure To Strengthen Industrial Refrigeration and Cold Chain Monitoring Systems Cybersecurity
WASHINGTON – Today, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the Department of Transportation (DOT) published a fact sheet that warns organizations of ongoing cyber threat activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems. Critical infrastructure sectors that widely use these systems include Healthcare and Public Health, Chemical, Food and Agriculture, and Transportation Systems.
Globally, malicious cyber actors are targeting vulnerabilities and weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities. If successfully exploited, the actors could change the temperature and possibly cause physical impacts such as fire hazards, loss of inventory and changes to the service life of the system. The fact sheet provides recommended best practices and protections against this threat activity such as:
- Remove control system devices and/or systems from the internet.
- Change default passwords and strengthen passwords.
- Apply patches and keep devices and systems updated.
- Identify, retire, and replace legacy devices that the vendor no longer supports.
“In close collaboration with our government, industry and international partners, CISA is actively tracking this threat activity,” said CISA Acting Executive Assistant Director for Cybersecurity Chris Butera. “Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target. We urge you to review the joint fact sheet and take action now to close known security gaps.”
“Industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems protect food, medicine, and other temperature-sensitive products, making them attractive targets for malicious cyber actors,” said FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman. “We are seeing these systems targeted across critical infrastructure sectors globally, putting inventory and equipment at risk. This fact sheet provides clear, practical steps that network defenders can take to reduce that risk and protect operations. The FBI urges every organization that relies on these systems to review our guidance, implement the recommended mitigations, and report any suspicious activity to the FBI.”
For more information on how to protect against cyber threats, visit Cybersecurity Best Practices.
###
About CISA
As the nation’s cyber defense agency and national coordinator for critical infrastructure security, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency leads the national effort to manage, uncover, and reduce risk to our digital and physical infrastructure Americans rely on every hour of every day.
Visit CISA.gov for more information and follow us on X, Facebook, LinkedIn, Instagram.
